class/VRService.d:
VRService is responsible for handling interactions between Roblox and Virtual Reality (VR). Its methods, properties, and events help you provide the best experience for end users seeking to experience Roblox on VR devices.

See VR Guidelines for more information on publishing an experience for VR devices.
class/VRService.s: Service responsible for handling interactions between Roblox and Virtual Reality (VR).

m.d: When set to VRScaling.World, Camera.HeadScale adjusts so that the scale of the world is seen from the avatar's perspective. A player with a small avatar will perceive the objects around them as larger than a player with a large avatar will.
m.s: Automatically adjusts scaling in VR to align the player with their avatar.

m.d:
When set to true, a VR player will be able to animate their hands and head using their controllers and headset. Set this to false for experiences where VR hand and head tracking conflicts with custom game mechanics, such as bespoke avatar rigs or weapon systems incompatible with IK-driven gestures.

This property must be set on the server.
m.s: When true, a VR player will be able to animate their hands and head using their controllers and headset.

m.d:
Controls how the models representing the player's VR hand controllers are displayed (VRControllerModelMode). When set to Transparent, the controller models are shown with transparency; when set to Disabled, the controller models are not rendered.

Defaults to Transparent.
m.s: Controls whether and how the player's VR hand controllers are rendered in the experience.

m.d: When true, a VR player's view fades to black when their head collides with an object. This property prevents players from being able to see through walls while in VR. The default value is true.
m.s: When true, a VR player's view will fade to black when their head collides with an object.

m.d:
This property describes what UserCFrame is responsible for input in VR. For instance, if a VR headset is responsible, the value of this property will be UserCFrame.Head.

To check if Roblox detects any VR devices, which would be responsible for input in VR, you can check the VREnabled property.
m.s: Describes what `Enum.UserCFrame` is responsible for input in VR.

m.d:
Controls the mode of the laser pointer that a VR player uses to point at and interact with the user interface (VRLaserPointerMode). Set it to Disabled to hide the laser pointer, Pointer to show a single pointer, or DualPointer to show a pointer for each hand.

Defaults to Pointer.
m.s: Controls whether and how the VR laser pointer used to interact with the user interface is displayed.

m.d: Read-only. Indicates whether the third-person follow camera is enabled for the VR user. Its value mirrors the user's VR comfort setting and updates automatically whenever the user changes that setting, firing a changed signal so that scripts can respond. It cannot be set from a script.
m.s: Indicates whether the third-person follow camera is enabled for the VR user.

m.d:
This property describes whether the user is using a virtual reality (VR) device.

If a VR device is enabled, you can interact with its location and movement through methods such as UserInputService:GetUserCFrame(). You can also react to VR device movement using the UserInputService.UserCFrameChanged event.

local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

local isUsingVR = UserInputService.VREnabled
if isUsingVR then
    print("User is using a VR headset!")
else
    print("User is not using a VR headset!")
end

This property can only be used in a LocalScript.

See Also

  • Camera.HeadLocked
  • UserInputService:GetUserCFrame()
  • UserInputService.UserCFrameChanged
m.s: Describes whether the user is using a virtual reality device.

m.d:
This method returns the VRTouchpadMode indicating the mode of a specified VRTouchpad. The returned mode indicates how the user interacts with their touchpad to play the game.

This can also be used alongside the several UserInputService VR methods and events.

This method will only work when used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Returns the VRTouchpadMode indicating the mode of a specified VRTouchpad.

p.s: The specified VRTouchpad.

r.s: The mode of the specified VRTouchpad.

m.d:
This method returns a CFrame describing the position and orientation of a specified virtual reality (VR) device as an offset from a point in real world space. This method should be used when implementing VR compatibility into a game to obtain and track the movement of a connected VR device.

By using the method, developers can implement features such as re-positioning the user's in-game character corresponding to the location of a connected VR device. This can be done by changing the CFrame of the user's in-game character to match the CFrame of the specified VR device using the UserCFrame enum and CFrame value arguments passed by the event.

VRService also provides a UserCFrameChanged event that automatically fires when the CFrame of connected VR device changes, so long it is used in a LocalScript.

This method will only work when used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Returns a CFrame describing the position & orientation of a specified virtual reality device as an offset from a point in real world space.

p.s: The specified UserCFrame.

r.s: A CFrame describing the position and orientation of the specified VR device as an offset from a point in real-world space.

m.d:
This method returns true if the specified UserCFrame virtual reality device (VR) is available to be listened to. It can be used to determine whether a specified VR device, such as UserCFrame.Head, is connected to the user's game.

This can also be used alongside the several UserInputService VR methods and events.

This method will only work when used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Returns true if the specified `Enum.UserCFrame` is available to be listened to.

p.s: The specified type of VR device.

r.s: A boolean indicating whether the specified VR device is enabled (true) or disabled (false).

m.d:
This method re-centers the CFrame of the user's head to the current location of the VR headset being worn by the user. It can be used to ensure that the user's in-game head is positioned according to the location of the user's VR headset.

This behaves identically to UserInputService:RecenterUserHeadCFrame().

This method will only work when used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Re-centers the `Datatype.CFrame` to the current location of the VR headset being worn by the user.

m.d:
This method requests navigation to the specified CFrame using the specified UserCFrame as the origin for the visualizer parabola. It can be used to incorporate virtual reality (VR) into your game by providing a means to visualize a navigation path from the user's VR device to a destination.

VRService has a similar event, NavigationRequested, used to detect such requests. This can also be used alongside the several UserInputService VR methods and events.

This method will only work when used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Requests navigation to the specified `Datatype.CFrame` using the specified `Enum.UserCFrame` as the origin for the visualizer parabola.

p.s: The specified CFrame coordinates.
The VR device for which the navigation is requested.

m.d:
This method sets the mode of the specified VRTouchpad to the specified VRTouchpadMode. It can be used to change the user's virtual reality (VR) touchpad mode so that the user interacts with the game differently using the touchpad.

This can also be used alongside the several UserInputService VR methods and events.

This method will only work when used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Sets the mode of the specified `Enum.VRTouchpad` to the specified `Enum.VRTouchpadMode`.

p.s: The specified VRTouchpad you want to set the mode of.
The mode you want to set the specified VRTouchpad to.

m.d:
This event fires when navigation is requested from VRService for a specified UserCFrame VR device. It fires with a CFrame coordinate and the specified UserCFrame indicating the device requesting the navigation.

This event can be used alongside UserInputService service events and methods.

Since this event fires locally, it can only be used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Fired when navigation is requested from `Class.VRService`.

p.s: The requested CFrame coordinates.
Indicates the VR device for which navigation is requested.

m.d:
This event fires if the VRTouchpadMode of a VRTouchpad is changed. You can use this event to track the states of VR touchpads connected via the user's client.

This event can be used alongside UserInputService service events and methods.

Since this event fires locally, it can only be used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Fires if the `Enum.VRTouchpadMode` of a `Enum.VRTouchpad` is changed.

p.s: The touchpad that changed mode.
The new mode.

m.d:
This event fires when a UserCFrame is changed, for instance when the user moves a connected VR device. It can be used alongside GetUserCFrame() to track the CFrame coordinates of a VR device, and when it changes/moves. It can also be used alongside UserInputService service events and methods.

Since this event fires locally, it can only be used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Fires when a `Enum.UserCFrame` is changed.

p.s: The type of VR device that changed.
The updated CFrame coordinates of the VR device after the change.

m.d:
This event fires when a UserCFrame is enabled or disabled. It can be used alongside GetUserCFrameEnabled() to track whether a specified UserCFrame is enabled, and when its state changes. It can also be used alongside UserInputService service events and methods.

Since this event fires locally, it can only be used in a LocalScript.
m.s: Fires when a `Enum.UserCFrame` is enabled or disabled.

p.s: The UserCFrame getting enabled or disabled.
A boolean indicating whether the UserCFrame is enabled (true) or disabled (false).

class/ValueBase.s: Base class of all "value instance" objects.

class/ValueCurve.d:
An instance representing a 1D value curve encoded via a sorted list of ValueCurveKeys. The shape of the interpolation curve between two keys is determined by the ValueCurveKey.Interpolation type.

Not all value types (for example, strings and other non-numerical types) may perform Linear or Cubic interpolation. These types will revert to Constant interpolation if necessary.
class/ValueCurve.s: A sorted list of time-value pairs that define a curve. Used to animate any type of value.

m.d: Number of keys in the value curve.
m.s: Number of keys in the value curve.

m.d: Read-only value indicating the type held in this curve, or the string "Nil" if there are no keys.
m.s: Read-only value indicating the type held in this curve.

m.d: Returns a copy of a key at a given index.
m.s: Returns a copy of a key at a given index.

p.s: The index in the existing set of keys held by this ValueCurve.

r.s: A copy of the ValueCurveKey stored at the given index.

m.d: The first item in the returned array is the index of the last key with time less than or equal to time (or the lesser of either 1 or the curve length if no key was found). The second item in the returned array is the index of the first key with time greater than or equal to time (or the curve length if no key was found satisfying the inequality).
m.s: Returns the index of the last and first key of a period of time.

p.s: A time during the animation. Inputs will be clamped between 0 and the time of the last key held by this ValueCurve.

r.s: An array of two indices bracketing time: the index of the last key at or before time, and the index of the first key at or after time.

m.d: Returns a copy of all the keys in the ValueCurve as a Luau array of ValueCurveKeys.
m.s: Returns a copy of all the keys in the ValueCurve as a Luau array of `Datatype.ValueCurveKey|ValueCurveKeys`.

r.s: Array of ValueCurveKeys.

m.d: Samples the value curve at a given time passed as argument.
m.s: Samples the value curve at a given time passed as argument.

p.s: Time at which to sample the curve.

r.s: Value of the curve at the requested time.

m.d:
Adds the key passed as an argument to this curve. If a key at the same time is found, it will be replaced. In the returned array, the first value is true if a key was added or false if a previous key was replaced; the second value is the index at which the marker was added.

If there are not yet any keys, then the key may be added. If keys exist, the type of the value must match those of existing keys; otherwise a message is printed and {false, -1} is returned.
m.s: Adds the key passed as an argument to this curve. If a key at the same time is found, it will be replaced.

p.s: ValueCurveKey to insert.

r.s: (see description)

m.d:
Creates a ValueCurveKey from the given arguments and inserts it in this curve. If a key at the same time is found, it will be replaced. In the returned array, the first value is true if a key was added or false if a previous key was replaced; the second value is the index at which the marker was added.

If there are not yet any keys, then the key may be added. If keys exist, the type of the value must match those of existing keys; otherwise a message is printed and {false, -1} is returned.
m.s: Creates a key for the given value and inserts it at the given time. If a key at the same time is found, it will be replaced.

p.s: Time at which to insert the new ValueCurveKey. - type: number
Value of the inserted ValueCurveKey. - type: any
Interpolation mode of the inserted ValueCurveKey. - type: KeyInterpolationMode

r.s: (see description)

m.d: Removes a given number (count) of keys starting from the startingIndex index and returns the number of keys that were removed.
m.s: Removes a given number of keys starting from a given index.

p.s: Starting index from which to remove keys.
Number of keys to remove.

r.s: Number of keys removed.

m.d:
Resets this curve's keys using the ValueCurveKey array passed as an argument. Keys in the keys array are sorted in ascending time order before insertion, and keys at duplicated times are removed in a stable manner.

Returns the number of keys actually inserted. Keys previously stored in this curve are removed before the keys passed as arguments are added.

The keys must all contain values of the same type. And that type must match any existing keys. Otherwise a message is printed, the keys are not added, and 0 is returned.
m.s: Resets this curve's keys using the `Datatype.ValueCurveKey` array passed as an argument.

p.s: Array of ValueCurveKeys.

r.s: Number of keys inserted.

class/Vector3Curve.d: Represents a 3D vector curve, grouping three FloatCurve instances. Each child FloatCurve can be accessed via the Vector3Curve:X(), Vector3Curve:Y(), and Vector3Curve:Z() methods. The three axes can be sampled simultaneously via the method Vector3Curve:GetValueAtTime().
class/Vector3Curve.s: Represents a 3D vector curve, grouping three `Class.FloatCurve` instances.

m.d: Returns the three FloatCurves (X, Y, Z) at the passed time argument as an array of three numbers. If a channel curve is missing or no key is found in the curve, the channel is evaluated as nil.
m.s: Returns the three `Class.FloatCurve|FloatCurves` (X, Y, Z) at the passed time argument.

p.s: Time at which to get the value.

r.s: The three FloatCurves (X, Y, Z) at the passed time argument.

m.d: Returns the FloatCurve controlling the X channel (the first child instance of type FloatCurve named X). If none is found, an empty FloatCurve is created.
m.s: Returns the `Class.FloatCurve` controlling the X channel (the first child instance of type `Class.FloatCurve` named `X`).

r.s: The FloatCurve controlling the X channel, or a newly created empty FloatCurve if none exists yet.

m.d: Returns the FloatCurve controlling the Y channel (the first child instance of type FloatCurve named Y). If none is found, an empty FloatCurve is created.
m.s: Returns the `Class.FloatCurve` controlling the Y channel (the first child instance of type `Class.FloatCurve` named `Y`).

r.s: The FloatCurve controlling the Y channel, or a newly created empty FloatCurve if none exists yet.

m.d: Returns the FloatCurve controlling the Z channel (the first child instance of type FloatCurve named Z). If none is found, an empty FloatCurve is created.
m.s: Returns the `Class.FloatCurve` controlling the Z channel (the first child instance of type `Class.FloatCurve` named `Z`).

r.s: The FloatCurve controlling the Z channel, or a newly created empty FloatCurve if none exists yet.

class/Vector3Value.d: A Vector3Value simply holds a Vector3 as a value. This value can be used for scripts to communicate, for objects to move to a preset location, etc.
class/Vector3Value.s: A container object for a single Vector3 value.

m.d: The stored Vector3.
m.s: The stored `Datatype.Vector3`.

m.d:
Fired whenever the Vector3Value.Value of the Vector3Value is changed. It will run with the new value being stored in the argument object, instead of a string representing the property being changed.

This event, like other changed events, can be used to track when an Vector3Value changes and to track the different values that it may change to.

For instance, this may be useful in games that rely on Vector3Values to track positions in the game world.

Equivalent changed events exist for similar objects, such as NumberValue and StringValue, depending on what object type best suits the need.
m.s: Fired whenever `Class.Vector3Value.Value` is changed.

p.s: The new value after the change.

m.dep: This deprecated event is a variant of Vector3Value.Changed which should be used instead.

class/VectorForce.d:
The VectorForce constraint applies constant force to an assembly. The direction and strength of the force is determined by a Vector3 and can be relative to an attachment on the part, another attachment, or the world coordinate system. Alternatively:

  • Because the VectorForce constraint applies constant force and acceleration, very high speeds may result if no other forces are involved. If you want to maintain a more steady velocity over time, use a LinearVelocity constraint.
  • If you only need initial velocity, set the AssemblyLinearVelocity property directly on the assembly.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Force Location

By default, force is applied to the assembly at the location of Attachment0. Thus, if its center of mass is not aligned with the direction/point of force, torque will be applied as well. If desired, force can be focused at the center of mass by toggling on ApplyAtCenterOfMass.

Relativity

By default, force is applied relative to Attachment0. If the parent assembly rotates, the force will change direction to match the adjusted orientation of the attachment; visualize this behavior in how the thruster of a rocket pushes it forward, regardless of the rocket's rotation.

If RelativeTo is set to World, force will be applied in world coordinates, independent of the parent or attachment orientations; visualize this behavior as a directional force like the wind blowing against an object.

If RelativeTo is set to Attachment1, force will be applied relative to Attachment1 and, if the attachment rotates, the force will change to match its orientation.
class/VectorForce.s: Applies constant force to an assembly.

m.d: When true, force is applied at the center of mass of the parent assembly of Attachment0. When false, force is applied at Attachment0.
m.s: Whether force is applied at the center of mass of the parent assembly.

kid.simple: If true, the push goes through the object's balance point, so it moves without spinning. If false (default), it pushes at Attachment0's spot, which can also make it twist if that spot is off-center.
kid.example:
local force = workspace.Box.VectorForce
force.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true -- push the middle, no tumbling

m.d: The strength and direction of the force.
m.s: The strength and direction of the force.

kid.simple: How hard and in which direction to push, as a Vector3. The length of the vector is the strength. Which way X, Y and Z point depends on RelativeTo.
kid.example:
local part = workspace.Box
local force = part.VectorForce
-- Push up with exactly the part's weight so it floats
force.Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity, 0)
kid.gotcha: Gravity is strong in Roblox (196.2). A Force of Vector3.new(0, 100, 0) on a normal-sized part will not lift it.

m.d: This property determines the CFrame in which the force is expressed.
m.s: The `Datatype.CFrame` in which the force is expressed.

kid.simple: Picks whose directions the Force uses. World: Y is always the sky. Attachment0 (default): directions turn with the part, like a rocket engine. Attachment1: directions follow the other attachment.
kid.example:
local force = workspace.Box.VectorForce
-- Wind that always blows toward +X, no matter how the box spins
force.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
force.Force = Vector3.new(500, 0, 0)
kid.gotcha: To fight gravity, use World. With Attachment0, if the part flips upside down your 'up' push becomes a 'down' push.

kid.simple: VectorForce is an invisible pusher that pushes a part with the same strength every moment, in a direction you choose. Because it never stops pushing, the part keeps speeding up, like a rocket. If you push up with exactly the part's weight, the part floats.
kid.analogy: VectorForce is like a rocket engine strapped to a box. The engine always pushes the same amount. With RelativeTo = Attachment0 it pushes wherever the box points (like a real rocket); with RelativeTo = World it always pushes one fixed direction (like wind).
whenToUse: Make a part hover by cancelling gravity
Wind that always blows one way
kid.where: Put it inside the part you want to push (or anywhere in workspace), with Attachment0 set to an attachment in that part. Works from a Script on the server. Make it with Instance.new("VectorForce").

terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.mass: How much 'stuff' an object has, which decides how hard it is to push. A part's mass = its volume x its material density. A 4x1x2 Plastic part (volume 8, density 0.7) has mass 5.6.
terms.gravity: The pull that makes things fall. In Roblox it is `workspace.Gravity`, which is 196.2 studs per second per second by default.
terms.acceleration: How fast speed changes. The rule is F = m x a (force = mass x acceleration). Push a mass-5.6 part with force 56 and it speeds up by 10 studs/s every second.
terms.velocity: Speed plus direction, written as a Vector3 in studs per second. Vector3.new(0, 0, 20) means 20 studs every second along the Z direction.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are rigidly joined (for example by welds) so they move as one solid object. A force on any part moves the whole group.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.attachment space: Directions measured using an attachment's own arrows. If the part tips over, 'up' for the attachment tips over too.
terms.RelativeTo: Chooses whose arrows the numbers use: World (the game world's fixed directions) or Attachment0/Attachment1 (that attachment's own directions, which turn when the part turns).
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Pushing exactly through it moves the object without spinning it; pushing off to the side also makes it spin.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.AssemblyMass: A part property that gives the total mass of the part plus every part welded to it. Use it to work out how much force you need.
terms.constant force: A push that never changes strength. Because F = m x a, a constant force gives a constant speed-up, so the part keeps getting faster and faster.

examples.title: Make a part hover in the air
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = false
part.Parent = workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local force = Instance.new("VectorForce")
force.Attachment0 = attachment
force.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World -- "up" means the sky
force.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true                 -- push the balance point, no spinning

-- Exactly cancel gravity: force = mass x gravity
force.Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity, 0)
force.Parent = part

print("Mass:", part.AssemblyMass)          -- 5.6 for a 4x1x2 Plastic part
print("Force needed:", force.Force.Y)      -- 5.6 x 196.2 = about 1098.7
explain: Gravity pulls down on the part with a force of mass x gravity. For a mass of 5.6 that is 5.6 x 196.2 = about 1098.7.
We push UP with exactly the same amount, so the two cancel out. The part stops falling and floats.
`RelativeTo = World` makes the Y in our Vector3 mean 'toward the sky', even if the part tips over.
`ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true` pushes through the balance point, so the part does not start spinning.
If you push a bit more (say 1.1 x the weight), the part slowly rises. A bit less, and it slowly sinks.

examples.title: A simple rocket that pushes where it points
examples.place: Script inside an unanchored Part named Rocket
examples.code:
local rocket = script.Parent

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = rocket

local thrust = Instance.new("VectorForce")
thrust.Attachment0 = attachment
-- Default RelativeTo is Attachment0: the force turns WITH the rocket
thrust.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.Attachment0
thrust.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true
-- Push up along the rocket's own Y arrow, twice as hard as gravity
thrust.Force = Vector3.new(0, rocket.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity * 2, 0)
thrust.Parent = rocket

task.wait(3)
thrust.Enabled = false -- engine off after 3 seconds; the rocket falls back
explain: With RelativeTo set to Attachment0, (0, number, 0) means 'along the rocket's own up arrow'. If the rocket tilts, the push tilts too.
We push with 2 x its weight. One weight cancels gravity, the extra weight speeds it upward.
After 3 seconds we switch the engine off with Enabled = false and gravity takes over.

gotchas: The part must be unanchored. Anchored parts ignore forces.
A VectorForce never lets go, so the part keeps getting faster. If you want a steady speed, use LinearVelocity instead.
Too-small numbers do nothing visible: a force of 10 on a part with mass 5.6 is weaker than gravity (about 1098.7), so the part still falls. Always compare with mass x gravity.
If the part spins wildly, turn on ApplyAtCenterOfMass, or put the attachment at the part's center.
Adding more welded parts increases AssemblyMass, so recalculate the force if your model changes.

class/VehicleController.d: A VehicleController is an object responsible for translating PlayerActions to movements with a VehicleSeat.
class/VehicleController.s: An object responsible for translating a seated player's directional input into throttle and steering for a `Class.VehicleSeat`.

class/VehicleSeat.d:
The VehicleSeat objects welds a player to the seat when the player touches the seat. It then forwards the movement inputs to any connected motor joints, allowing control of a vehicle.

While VehicleSeat is great for making simple vehicles they do have some limitations. Movement control will only detect motors connected directly to the vehicle seat, or through another rigid connection. This means that if you have a wheel connected to a beam which is then welded to the seat it will work fine, however if you have the wheel connected to a part, which is connected by a hinge to the rest of the car, it will not work.
class/VehicleSeat.s: A seat object that can be used to control a vehicle.

m.d: Displays how many hinges are detected by the VehicleSeat. Useful for debugging vehicle designs.
m.s: Displays how many hinges are detected by the `VehicleSeat`. Useful for debugging vehicle designs.

m.d: Toggles whether the VehicleSeat is active or not. If the seat is disabled, it will not automatically weld a character to it on collision and will not allow a character to control the connected vehicle.
m.s: Toggles whether the `VehicleSeat` is active or not.

m.d: If true, a UI speed bar will be displayed on screen that tells you what speed the vehicle is moving at.
m.s: If `true`, a UI speed bar will be displayed on screen that tells you what speed the vehicle is moving at.

m.d: The maximum speed that can be attained.
m.s: The maximum speed that can be attained.

m.d: The Humanoid that is sitting in the seat.
m.s: The `Class.Humanoid` that is sitting in the seat.

m.d: The direction of movement, tied to left and right movement inputs. Can be either 1 (right), 0 (straight), or -1 (left). Will refresh back to 0 unless constantly set.
m.s: The direction of movement, tied to left and right movement inputs.
m.dep: This property is no longer replicated and has been deprecated in favor of SteerFloat which is a float variant and should be used instead.

m.d: The left-to-right movement float, tied to left and right movement inputs. Can range between 1 (right) and -1 (left). Will refresh back to 0 (straight) unless constantly set.
m.s: The left-to-right movement float, tied to left and right movement inputs.

m.d: The direction of throttle, tied to forward and backward movement inputs. Can be either 1 (forward), 0 (null), or -1 (reverse). Will refresh back to 0 unless constantly set.
m.s: The direction of throttle, tied to forward and backward movement inputs.
m.dep: This property is not longer replicated and has been deprecated in favor of ThrottleFloat which is a float variant and should be used instead.

m.d: The forward-to-reverse throttle float, tied to forward and backward movement inputs. Can range between 1 (forward) and -1 (reverse). Will refresh back to 0 (null) unless constantly set.
m.s: The forward-to-reverse throttle float, tied to forward and backward movement inputs.

m.d: How fast the vehicle will be able to attain MaxSpeed. The greater the number, the faster it will reach the maximum speed.

class/VideoFrame.d:
A VideoFrame renders a rectangle, like a Frame does, with a moving video image. The video must be from a file uploaded to the Roblox website.

The video is scaled to fit the entirety of the rectangle, but looks best when displayed at its native resolution.

2D and 3D Sound

A VideoFrame placed underneath SurfaceGui on a BasePart will emit its sound from that part's BasePart.Position.

A VideoFrame exhibits the Doppler effect, meaning its frequency and pitch varies with the relative motion of whatever part it is attached to.

The volume of the VideoFrame will be determined by the distance between the client's sound listener (by default the Camera position) and the position of the VideoFrame's part.

A VideoFrame is considered "global" if it is not placed underneath SurfaceGui on a BasePart. In this case, the sound will play at the same volume throughout the entire place.
class/VideoFrame.s: A GUI object that renders a rectangle, like a `Class.Frame` does, with a moving video image.

class/ViewportFrame.d:
ViewportFrame is a GuiObject that renders 3D objects inside its bounds, offering a way to display 3D objects in a 2D space like a ScreenGui. This object has the following caveats:

  • No shadows or post-processing effects are rendered.

  • Material.Neon and Material.Glass materials render at the lowest quality.

  • Nested GuiObjects aren't supported.

  • By default, lighting inside a ViewportFrame acts as if Lighting.EnvironmentSpecularScale and Lighting.EnvironmentDiffuseScale are both set to 0, so properties that rely on these fields, such as SurfaceAppearance.MetalnessMap, may look different.

  • This object can use a Sky child as a cubemap for reflections, in which case only the Sky object's six Skybox[…] properties are used. Assuming these properties are valid, lighting inside the ViewportFrame acts similarly to if Lighting.EnvironmentSpecularScale and Lighting.EnvironmentDiffuseScale are both set to 1. For details, see here.
class/ViewportFrame.s: `Class.GuiObject` that renders 3D objects inside its bounds.

m.d: This property determines the lighting hue applied to the area within the ViewportFrame. Defaults to Color3.fromRGB(200, 200, 200) (ghost grey).
m.s: The lighting hue applied to the area within the `ViewportFrame`.

m.d:
Camera instance that is used to render children objects. Defaults to nil.

The Camera object does not replicate so the ViewportFrame.CurrentCamera won't replicate either. When you set this property, Camera.CFrame and Camera.FieldOfView will be saved and replicate with the ViewportFrame internally so the client can render the frame without a Camera object.
m.s: `Class.Camera` that is used to render children objects.

m.d:
This property determines how the rendered viewport image will be colorized, allowing you to change the color without directly modifying the rendered object. The default colorization value is Color3.new(1, 1, 1) (white) at which no color modification occurs.

See also ImageTransparency which determines the transparency of the rendered image.
m.s: Determines how the rendered viewport image will be colorized.

m.d:
This property determines the transparency of the rendered viewport image, allowing you to change the transparency without directly modifying the rendered object. A value of 0 (default) is completely opaque and a value of 1 is completely transparent (invisible).

See also ImageColor3 which determines how the rendered image will be colorized.
m.s: Determines the transparency of the rendered viewport image.

m.s: The color of the emitted light.

class/VirtualInput.d:
VirtualInput simulates mouse, keyboard, and pointer input as if it were performed by a real player. It is intended for testing purposes only and can only be obtained by calling UserInputService:CreateVirtualInput().

All input methods throw a runtime error if the simulated input would interact with Roblox's built-in UI (CoreGui), such as the top bar, chat window, or escape menu. This prevents automation tests from accidentally interfering with system UI that players depend on.
class/VirtualInput.s: Simulates mouse, keyboard, and pointer input as if it were performed by a real player.

m.d:
This method injects a keyboard key press or release event, processed identically to a real hardware key event.

This method throws a runtime error if CoreGui has keyboard focus, which includes a TextBox inside CoreGui being focused, a CoreGui element selected for keyboard or gamepad navigation, or the in-game escape menu being open. It also throws if the requested key is permanently bound to a Roblox core action (for example, the Escape key).

isRepeatedKey

Set isRepeatedKey to true only when simulating the OS auto-repeat behavior that occurs while a player physically holds a key down which fires a stream of repeated events after the initial key press. This is meaningful only for text-manipulation keys: KeyCode.Backspace, KeyCode.Delete, and the arrow keys (KeyCode.Left, KeyCode.Right, KeyCode.Up, and KeyCode.Down). Passing true for any other key throws a runtime error.

For example, to simulate holding Backspace to delete multiple characters, call:

  • SendKey(true, Enum.KeyCode.Backspace, false) for the initial press
  • SendKey(true, Enum.KeyCode.Backspace, true) in a loop for each repeated event
  • SendKey(false, Enum.KeyCode.Backspace, false) for the release

Do not pass isRepeatedKey as true for the initial press or the release. For any key that does not involve text editing (game action keys, modifier keys, function keys, etc.), always pass false.
m.s: Injects a keyboard key press or release event.

p.s: Whether to simulate a key press (true) or a key release (false).
The KeyCode of the key to inject.
Whether this is an auto-repeat event, as occurs when a key is held down. Only valid for text-manipulation keys such as KeyCode.Backspace, KeyCode.Delete, and the arrow keys. Defaults to false.

m.d:
This method injects a mouse button press or release event at the given screen-space position, processed identically to a real hardware mouse event.

Only UserInputType.MouseButton1, UserInputType.MouseButton2, and UserInputType.MouseButton3 are supported; passing any other value throws a runtime error.

This method throws a runtime error if the specified position overlaps an interactive CoreGui element such as a button or an active overlay in the top bar, chat window, or escape menu. It also throws if the specified button is already in the requested state, for example pressing a button that is already pressed.
m.s: Injects a mouse button press or release event at the specified screen position.

p.s: The screen-space position in pixels at which to inject the event.
The mouse button to use. Supported values are UserInputType.MouseButton1, UserInputType.MouseButton2, and UserInputType.MouseButton3.
Whether to simulate a button press (true) or a button release (false).
The consecutive-click count for multi-click detection, such as a double- or triple-click. Defaults to 0.

m.d:
This method injects a relative mouse movement event, representing how far the mouse moved rather than where it is on screen. This is intended for use while the player's cursor is locked, such as in first-person camera mode.

This method throws a runtime error when the cursor is not locked. To move the cursor to an absolute screen position instead, use SendMousePosition().
m.s: Injects a relative mouse movement event. Only works while the player's cursor is locked.

p.s: The relative mouse movement in pixels along each axis.

m.d:
This method moves the virtual mouse cursor to the specified absolute screen-space position, processed identically to a real hardware mouse-move event.

This method throws a runtime error when the specified position overlaps an interactive Roblox UI element (such as a button or active overlay in the top bar, chat window, or escape menu).

To inject relative mouse movement while the cursor is locked, use SendMouseDelta() instead.
m.s: Moves the virtual mouse cursor to the specified absolute screen position.

p.s: The target screen-space position in pixels.

m.d:
This method injects a pointer action event at the given screen-space position. The pointerAction dictionary accepts the following keys:

  • Wheel (number) — Scroll wheel delta. Positive values scroll forward, negative values scroll backward.
  • Pan (Vector2) — Trackpad pan delta in pixels.
  • Pinch (number) — Pinch-to-zoom delta. Positive values zoom in, negative values zoom out.

This method throws a runtime error if the specified position overlaps an interactive Roblox UI element (such as a button or active overlay in the top bar, chat window, or escape menu). If all values in pointerAction are zero, the call returns without injecting any event.
m.s: Injects a scroll wheel, trackpad pan, or pinch gesture event at the specified screen position.

p.s: The screen-space position in pixels at which to inject the event.
A dictionary describing the pointer action to inject. Accepted keys are Wheel (number), Pan (Vector2), and Pinch (number). At least one key must have a non-zero value.

m.d:
This method injects a text input event, routing the given string directly to the focused TextBox or the experience's text input handler as if the player typed it on a physical keyboard. This is useful for populating text fields without needing to simulate individual key presses.

This method throws a runtime error if CoreGui has keyboard focus, which includes a TextBox inside CoreGui being focused, a CoreGui element selected for keyboard or gamepad navigation, or the in-game escape menu being open.
m.s: Injects a text input event as if the specified string was typed on a keyboard.

p.s: The string to inject as text input.

class/VirtualInputManager.d: VirtualInputManager is an internal service used by Roblox to record inputs and play them back during performance benchmarking tests.
class/VirtualInputManager.s: An internal service that offers no functionality to developers.

class/VirtualUser.d: VirtualUser is a service that allows you to record the inputs of a user, and then play it back to a limited extent. This service hasn't been maintained in several years, so it doesn't work very well anymore.
class/VirtualUser.s: VirtualUser is a service that allows you to record the inputs of a user, and then play it back to a limited extent.

class/VisibilityCheckDispatcher.d:
Not accessible from scripts. VisibilityCheckDispatcher measures the viewability of on-screen ads, such as those rendered by AdGui. On every RunService heartbeat, it selects pending ad instances and runs the on-screen and occlusion checks that determine whether an ad impression should be counted, then reports the results through AdService.

This service is created and managed by the engine.
class/VisibilityCheckDispatcher.s: Service that schedules and runs viewability checks for immersive ad instances in a place.

class/Visit.d: The Visit service is a backend service used by Roblox. Its functions are not accessible to developers in any form.
class/Visit.s: The Visit service is a backend service used by Roblox. Its functions are not accessible to developers in any form.

class/VoiceChatService.d: VoiceChatService is responsible for voice chat's high-level functionality. This mostly consists of configuration options, and functions that are not specifically-controlled by more-specific instances.
class/VoiceChatService.s: **VoiceChatService** is responsible for voice chat's high-level functionality.

m.d:
This property controls the default distance attenuation curve assigned to any generated AudioEmitter instances in the default voice chat setup.

This property only has an effect if EnableDefaultVoice and UseAudioApi are both enabled, since no AudioEmitters are otherwise generated.
m.s: Determines which distance attenuation curve the default voice chat setup uses when `Class.AudioDeviceInput` and `Class.AudioEmitter` objects are generated.

m.d:
When enabled, each voice-eligible player can be heard as though they were speaking through their character. The implementation details of the voice setup depend on UseAudioApi.

When UseAudioApi is Enabled, disabling this property disables the default setup, but AudioDeviceInput will still work. Conversely, when UseAudioApi is Disabled, disabling the default voice setup effectively disables voice chat altogether.
m.s: Controls whether each voice-eligible player can be heard as though they were speaking through their character.

m.d:
This RolloutState property controls whether Roblox's built-in voice chat volume controls are available to players, including a global voice chat volume slider and per-user volume adjustments.

When set to Enabled, these controls are available to players. When set to Disabled, the built-in controls are hidden, though creators can still implement their own custom voice volume controls. Default follows the default for this feature.

If UseAudioApi is disabled, this property has no effect and built-in controls will be hidden.
m.s: Controls whether Roblox's built-in voice chat volume controls are available to players.

m.d:
If Enabled, the voice chat setup is represented and controlled by AudioDeviceInput objects. More specifically:

  • An AudioDeviceInput will be created and parented to each voice-eligible Player.
  • An AudioEmitter will be created and parented to each voice-eligible player's Player.Character.
  • An AudioListener will be created and parented to Workspace.CurrentCamera.

You can disable the default setup by setting VoiceChatService.EnableDefaultVoice to false.

If Disabled, the voice chat setup is done through an internal-only system.

Currently, setting this to Automatic has the same meaning as Disabled. However, in the future, Automatic will become Enabled, so that new experiences can achieve greater customization over voice.
m.s: Controls whether voice chat is represented and controlled by `Class.AudioDeviceInput` objects.

m.d:
Returns a sorted array of arrays of chat group IDs for the given players. Each chat group ID is a string that represents a communication-compatible group within the current universe.

If two or more players share the same chat group ID, those players are eligible to voice chat with each other based on their age-check status, voice chat eligibility, and communication settings.

This method is server-side only and intended for real-time use cases such as matchmaking and teleporting. Chat group IDs are unique to the current universe, may change over time, and should not be stored once the user has left the experience. While you can hold onto the data returned for the purposes of gameplay while the user is in the experience, this data should not be stored after they've left.

To use this method, you must enable Chat & Voice Groups APIs in Experience Settings ⟩ Communication in Roblox Studio and agree to the Roblox Terms of Use.

In Roblox Studio this API is only available when the experience is running in Team Test.
m.s: Returns chat group IDs that indicate which players can voice chat together.

p.s: A list of Players currently in the experience to evaluate for voice chat compatibility.

r.s: A sorted array of arrays of chat group ID strings. Players who share a matching chat group ID are eligible to voice chat with each other.

m.d:
Returns whether or not the given user has voice enabled. On the client-side, this can only be used to check the voice status of the local player. On the server-side, this can only check the voice status for players in that server.

This function can throw an error if the HTTP call fails.
m.s: Returns whether or not the given user has voice enabled.

p.s: The Player.UserId to check.

r.s: If that user has voice enabled.
